newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Philips has 1996 net loss but sees recovery.
newsitem.headline: Philips has 1996 net loss but sees recovery.

text.p: Philips Electronics NV on Thursday reported its first net annual loss since 1992, but vowed profits would return to customary levels this year.
Huge restructuring and one-off charges plus stubbornly difficult market conditions plunged the Dutch electronics giant, whose product range spans shavers to semiconductors, into the red.
It reported a 1996 net loss of 590 million guilders ($312.2 million), compared with a 1995 net profit of 2.52 billion, after net extraordinary charges of 1.3 billion.
Net profit from normal operations were 723 million guilders, down from 2.68 billion in 1995, and way below analysts' forecasts for a profit ranging from 1.09 billion to 1.53 billion guilders.
The dividend was unchanged at 1.60 guilders per common share.

"We have decided to pay a dividend equal to last year's because we are confident that we will produce a result in 1997 which is in line with normal expectations," Cor Boonstra told his first annual results news conference since becoming chairman last October.
"The year 1996 was a severe disappointment, due to a much lower level of sales growth and costs which grew at a faster rate than sales," Philips said in a statement.

But the company forecast its current businesses would continue to grow in 1997. "We are committed to a return to profitability and to the achievement of a positive cash flow of over one billion guilders," Boonstra said.

He acknowledged the effect of the extraordinary items and said Philips had not responded quickly enough to market conditions. "Part of this decline was caused by gearing up our organisation for growth which did not materialise. We were simply not quick enough in reacting to the market," he said.
"We do not blame the markets, nor our competitors, but rather take full responsibility for our lack of speed," he said.

Charges taken during the year included an 800 million guilder pre-tax charge to restructure the Sound and Vision unit and one billion guilders, of which 600 million related to loss-making German unit Grundig.
Philips has deconsolidated Grundig and from this year will no longer pick up the tab for losses at the company, accounting for it only on a pro-rata basis for its 32 percent stake.

Philips is currently focusing on existing core businesses rather than moving into new areas. "At this stage we are focusing on building our 100 existing businesses, rather than acquiring businesses in new areas or strategically reshaping the portfolio," Boonstra said.
Boonstra repeated his policy of weeding out the company's underperformers and loss-makers.
"While this process is not yet complete, it is on schedule, and we are rapidly disposing of activities that absorb profits, cash and management time," he said.
He poured cold water on speculation in financial markets that he was preparing to split the company up.

Market watchers and some analysts have speculated that Boonstra might be tempted to maximise value to Philips shareholders by splitting up the company and going forward in a drastically pared-down form.
Boonstra said the relationship with 75 percent-owned music and films group PolyGram NV was not under review, answering speculation the unit would be put up for sale.

He repeated Philips' commitment to its troubled Sound and Vision unit, which makes televisions and audio equipment. "There's not a serious consideration, there's not even an unserious consideration, to change our relationship with Sound and Vision," he said.
Philips had a fourth quarter net loss from normal operations of 81 million guilders after a profit of 1.02 billion guilders in the fourth quarter of 1995.
Analysts had expected Philips to report fourth quarter net profit from normal operations of 387-750 million guilders, with consensus around 526 million.

"The figures were not as good as expected, but not terribly disappointing. It is a good idea Philips is taking all the charges now," said Peter Wortel of Delta Lloyd Bank. "1997 will probably still be tough, but in 1998 the effects of all the restructuring should start working out for Philips."

Eric de Graaf of ING Barings said his firm was sticking to its buy recommendation. "We believe in the sector and we think that Boonstra is walking the right path. If he cuts away the bad parts, the rest will be good," he said.

Shares in Philips initially hovered around Wednesday's closing level of 78.10 guilders after the results came out but by 1200 GMT the shares were off 30 cents at 77.80 guilders. ($ = 1.889 Dutch Guilders)
